articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.title_zh: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks , this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.
Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war , fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.
The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too  — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years .
To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.
“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.
It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine . But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”
Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.
Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”
Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.
Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.
Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if  that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.
“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves  said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.
“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”
Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”
Security guarantees for  Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”
European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.
Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”
Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”
Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.
“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”
Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.
If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.
He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.
Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.
The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”
Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.
The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.
Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.
There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.
“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.
He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string

articles.title_orig: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.title_zh: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.content_orig:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles. However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted. Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either. Google may use this data in other ways for up to three years—it just won’t add it to AI-training data sets.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now. Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user). Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months. So you can access that data for longer, but so can Google. The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement. Google says the change is rolling out globally, but it may take a few weeks to show up for everyone.

articles.title_orig: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: CA DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after Bay Area traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.title_zh: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.content_orig:
Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.
The lawsuit was brought about by Alex Neill, who is representing consumers that purchased PlayStation digital content between August 2016 and February 2026. The action accused PlayStation of having a ‘near monopoly’ on digital games and add-on content on PlayStation platforms. The case argued that Sony sets strict terms and conditions on developers, and charges a 30% commission on every purchase, which results in “excessive and unfair prices”. It claimed the prices are out of proportion to the costs.
But London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected this, and said the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law. As a result, it has dismissed the case in its entirety.
Join The Game Business Today!
The lawsuit argued that once you own a PlayStation, you are trapped within the ecosystem. The Tribunal disagreed, and ruled that Sony competes within a wider ‘systems market’ with the likes of Xbox, Nintendo and PC. It also ruled that gamers can buy physical games (at least for now).
The court said that forcing PlayStation to allow third-party stores onto the platform would be expensive, complex and could impact security. It added that under competition law, there was no legal duty for Sony to do this.
Finally, the court didn’t find pricing to be unfair. It said that Alex Neill had failed to prove Sony’s profit margins were excessive, especially as console makers sell hardware cheaply to make money back on game sales. Furthermore, there tribunal said there no evidence that rival stores would have brought pricing down.
PlayStation still faces similar class actions in Australia, Netherlands and Portugal at an earlier stage.
For more details on the Alex Neill case, you can read our run-down from earlier this year.
The Game Business is a reader-supported publication. Join us today!
Sony's digital store has always charged significantly more than physical stores, despite digital obviously having lower production costs/overheads.
Forcing Sony to allow alternate stores isn't the answer but forcing Sony to allow retailers to sell digital codes would have been a fair compromise, potentially recreating the pre-digital dynamic.
Not only would this result in positive pricing competition, it might allow the games retail scene to grow again, and help sustain nice shops/third spaces for gamers to come together rather than it all be done online.
Perhaps current competition law isn't equipped to deal with the digital age and needs to be reviewed?

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.
The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.
Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.
Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks slid lower, pulling the Nasdaq index down more than 1 percent. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.

articles.title_orig: Trump is heading to China for APEC amid renewed calls to curb Nvidia chip sales. Here's what to watch
articles.title_zh: Trump is heading to China for APEC amid renewed calls to curb Nvidia chip sales. Here's what to watch
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

articles.title_orig: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.title_zh: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.content_orig:
A hacker responsible for high-profile cyberattacks, including stealing footage from Grand Theft Auto VI in the hope of blackmailing its publisher, pleaded guilty to several crimes, British prosecutors said.
Arion Kurtaj, 21, pleaded guilty to cybercrimes including illegally impairing computer systems, as well as to fraud, Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service said in a news release on Monday.
“His offending was calculated,” said Robert Hutchinson, a prosecutor, adding that even after being charged, Mr. Kurtaj continued to break the law.
He will be sentenced on Monday in a London court, prosecutors said. Mr. Kurtaj’s publication in 2022 of footage illustrating the gameplay of Grand Theft Auto VI, a closely guarded sequel 13 years in the making, sent shock waves through the industry.
The recent guilty plea was another turn in a long case against Mr. Kurtaj, who was found unfit to stand trial before that finding was reversed.
Prosecutors said he was a member of a hacking group, Lapsus$, and that he had launched attacks on several companies while he was still a teenager.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.title_zh: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.content_orig:
The Civilization and XCOM developer is shrinking as a new XCOM game has missed a development milestone, according to Bloomberg
Take-Two Interactive $TTWO 's Firaxis Games cut roughly 60 jobs on Tuesday, about one-third of the studio's workforce, according to Bloomberg .
A spokesperson from 2K Games, the Take-Two imprint that oversees Firaxis, verified that Heather Hazen, who heads the studio, is departing, according to Bloomberg. The Maryland-based studio makes the Civilization and XCOM franchises.
"Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength — designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," the spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis."
The spokesperson described Hazen’s exit as a planned handover, according to Game Developer . “With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start,” the spokesperson said, according to Game Developer.
Firaxis has been working on a new XCOM title that ran into development problems and fell short of an important milestone this summer, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing unnamed people, said work on the game will go on, though the cuts could bring major changes to it.
“Civilization VII,” the studio’s latest title, came out last year to a lukewarm response and has been patched repeatedly since, according to Bloomberg. The game holds a 51% positive user rating on Steam, according to Kotaku .
The layoffs land just two days prior to “Grand Theft Auto VI” hitting the market, according to Bloomberg. Rockstar, a separate Take-Two label, develops and publishes that game.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Breaks Silence, Signals Willingness to Return as Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Breaks Silence, Signals Willingness to Return as Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia .
The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier.
Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August.
By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear.
Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight.
Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported .
Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis.
A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence.
Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war .
"Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses .
Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance.
Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even "calls me in the middle of the night."
It wasn't always that way.
At Trump's Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn't there. The two men had never met.
That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company's market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters .
Two days before the meeting, Trump's money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock .
For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia's H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge , according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China's development of its own.
The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales . A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company's chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day.
Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump's international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump's inaugural fund , would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported .
But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported .
Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia's business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips . His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after.
In the first eight months of 2026, Trump's accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC's analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone.
Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job , the Times reported.
With Huang out and Nvidia's shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a "tremendous talent" who was "going through hell" — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market's record highs.
Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him "certainly isn't a bad idea." But Nvidia's board is not considering his return , a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because they were discussing internal matters."

articles.title_zh: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.content_orig:

Chinese authorities have sacked the researcher who led an experimental gene-editing trial that resulted in the death of a child . An investigation into the trial by the Shanghai municipal government found that the researcher and his team failed to follow regulations and overlooked warning signs in a safety report. Several others involved in the case have also been punished.
Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next
Two children died from gene therapies in China: where the field goes next
In July, the journal Science and the website Retraction Watch jointly reported that Zilong Qiu, a neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, led a team that developed an experimental gene-editing therapy for a six-year-old girl with a rare neurodevelopmental disorder called Snijders Blok–Campeau syndrome. The therapy was carried by a viral vector that was injected into the girl’s spine and then travelled to her brain. The girl died of medical complications after receiving the therapy at Xinhua Hospital, also in Shanghai, in March 2025.
The institutions involved in the trial — Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital — have also been reprimanded and instructed to examine their own practices. “I expect the action to send a big warning to research institutes and hospitals across the country,” says Jiayou Shi, a lawyer at the National Research Center for Civil and Commercial Law at Renmin University of China in Beijing.
The trial was conducted under China’s fast-track pathway , called investigator-initiated trials (IITs). IITs allow researchers and biotech companies to test therapies quickly in hospitals without supervision from the country’s regulators. The Chinese government increased oversight of these trials in May, which Shi says should prevent similar cases in future.
Lizzi Lee, who studies China’s economic and technological policies at the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York City, says the trial is “a cautionary tale” for the country’s rapidly growing biotechnology industry. There is real momentum in the industry in China, but clinical oversight hasn’t always kept pace, Lee says. “The investigation is quite candid about what went wrong,” adds Lee.
According to a statement released through China’s state-run media on 13 November, the Shanghai government’s investigation found that Qiu was the main person responsible for the research. He has been sacked from his position as the deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institution, which is affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Another member of Qiu’s team, a deputy researcher at Xinhua Hospital, has also been dismissed. Both researchers have been barred from leading or participating in science projects for five years and have been added to a national database of people and organizations that have committed serious breaches of research integrity.
About a month before the girl received the experimental therapy , Qiu’s team received results from a preclinical toxicology study showing that monkeys sustained liver damage, according to Science and Retraction Watch. Investigators found that Qiu’s team failed to inform the researcher in charge of the clinical research at Xinhua Hospital in a timely fashion about the results of the primate experiment, which meant “the early warning signal” in the safety report was not “given high attention”, according to the statement. The clinical researcher has been removed as head of research at Xinhua Hospital. Qiu did not respond to questions about the investigation report.
Shi says the trial in the girl should not have gone ahead if the therapy showed evidence of harm in animals.
The investigators also found that Xinhua Hospital failed to conduct sufficient scientific assessment for the clinical trial. According to the statement, although the hospital’s ethics committee asked the research team to submit extra materials when safety evidence was lacking, it approved the trial without receiving those materials. In addition, the consent form given to the children’s family did not mention death as a risk of taking the therapy. Two members of the hospital’s ethics committee were given penalties.
Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine and Xinhua Hospital did not respond to questions about the investigation report.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.title_zh: Kalshi takes down controversial Trump 'mention' markets at CFTC's request
articles.content_orig:
Kalshi is pausing markets that allow users to bet on what President Trump will say in response to a federal agency's request, a spokesperson for the prediction market confirmed.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission requested that Kalshi halt the so-called "mention markets" tied to the president on Friday.
Mention markets allow traders to bet on specific words or phrases a person will utter during public events, such as speeches or earnings calls. Users often spend hours researching a person's speech patterns to make an informed guess about what they might say.
"We are complying with the order," the Kalshi spokesperson said in an email. The company will still allow some mention markets related to the Trump administration, according to The Wall Street Journal, which earlier reported the pause.
Reached for comment, a CFTC spokesperson said the decision was consistent with a September order that stayed the certification of certain mention markets by Kalshi.
"These contract types present a heightened risk of manipulation because their settlement turns on the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable," the agency said at the time.
The CFTC's order follows a July incident in which a White House teleprompter operator made more than $100,000 on Kalshi bets tied to public speeches by President Trump. The trading activity by an administration employee fueled concerns about insider trading on prediction market platforms, an issue that has attracted lawmakers' attention .
Kalshi said it updated its rules in March to better detect insider trading and prevent market manipulation.
Kalshi has removed other markets at the CFTC's behest in the past. In August, the company removed all sports-related mention markets, which previously generated $90 million in monthly trading volume, according to a person familiar with the matter.

articles.title_orig: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.title_zh: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.content_orig:
Hungary’s new anti-corruption agency made an eye-catching splash last week when it released photographs of a table piled with bank notes worth nearly $20 million. The money, the agency said, had been found hidden in forests and farm buildings during a hunt for funds stolen during the long tenure of the country’s former prime minister, Viktor Orban.
This week, Hungary’s new leader, Peter Magyar, announced that the stacks of cash photographed by the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up as part of what he calls “operation cleansing fire,” were just the “tip of the iceberg.”
To display the full volume of money ransacked by corrupt officials before Mr. Orban lost a general election in April , Mr. Magyar told Parliament on Monday, “You would have to put 10,000 tables next to each other.”
In his telling, the total amounts to more than 60 trillion Hungarian forint (more than $180 billion) — a staggering, and so far unproven, sum in a small Eastern European country whose total spending on defense last year was around only $5 billion.
While Mr. Magyar is prone to exaggeration by character and political calculus, his angry denunciations of Orban-era corruption resonate with many Hungarians and helped his party win the April election.
Mr. Orban and his die-hard supporters have dismissed the photographs of recovered cash and a rash of detentions as hollow political theater aimed at discrediting and destroying opposition to Mr. Magyar, who was sworn in as prime minister in May.

Ukrainian forces struck a military airfield in Russia's Astrakhan Oblast and a site used to store, prepare, and launch drones in Oryol Oblast on Nov. 15, Ukraine's General Staff said.
In Astrakhan Oblast, drones targeted the Akhtubinsk airfield, which hosts Russia's 929th State Flight Test Center , one of the country's main facilities for testing new military aircraft and weapons, the General Staff said.
Russia uses the airfield to station Su-34 fighter-bombers , which carry out attacks on Ukrainian cities and military positions using glide bombs .
A powerful secondary explosion was recorded at an ammunition depot storing components for guided aerial missiles following the strike, according to the General Staff.
Earlier on Nov. 15, the Telegram channel Exilenova Plus said that after the detonation, at least 30 explosions were heard on site.
Ukrainian forces also hit a mobile PRV-13 radar altimeter, a system used to measure aircraft altitude and determine their coordinates.
The airbase lies around 650 kilometers (400 miles) east of the Ukrainian-controlled territory , some 30 kilometers (less than 20 miles) west of Russia's border with Kazakhstan .
Astrakhan Oblast Governor Igor Babushkin said that 31 drones were destroyed in the northern part of the region overnight.
The second target was a drone storage, preparation, and launch site known as the Tsymbulova drone port, near the settlement of Tsimbulova in Russia's Oryol Oblast .
Russian forces use the site to launch attack drones against Ukrainian cities, civilian and energy infrastructure , the General Staff said.
Russian forces attacked energy infrastructure in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad oblasts overnight and on the morning of Nov. 15 alone, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky .
Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs, and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week.
Only over the past day, at least four civilians were killed, while 69 others were injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine.
The Akhtubinsk airfield has been targeted by Ukraine before.
Russian Sukhoi Su-57 fifth-generation fighter jet was damaged at Akhtubinsk airfield on Oct. 29, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) confirmed .
On Aug. 20, a Ukrainian drone strike damaged a Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber stationed in Akhtubinsk, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
In separate attacks, Ukrainian forces struck three Russian military-industrial facilities overnight on Nov. 15, including two major petrochemical and oil refining plants in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan and a helicopter manufacturer in Bryansk Oblast.

Russia's growing dependence on China is reshaping one of the world's most important geopolitical relationships. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the resulting Western sanctions, Russia has relied heavily on Beijing for trade, technology and critical imports. Along the vast Russia-China border, economic cooperation is expanding, but experts warn that the relationship is increasingly unequal, giving China significant leverage.
DW explores historical tensions, Russian security concerns, reports of espionage and the strategic risks facing Russia as China's influence grows, raising questions about the future of the countries' much-publicized "no-limits" partnership.

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.
Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.
As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.
A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.
Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”
Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.
During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”
It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos , who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.
The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.
During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”
India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.
The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. On Tuesday, shares of technology companies in Asia tumbled after the Trump administration announced rules to restrict overseas access to advanced A.I. chips like those sold by Nvidia. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

articles.title_orig: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.title_zh: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.title_zh: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.content_orig:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

articles.title_orig: Christmas Island Is Suddenly Awash in Red
articles.title_zh: Christmas Island Is Suddenly Awash in Red
articles.content_orig: Roughly 100 million Red Crabs are currently in the middle of their famous annual migration across Australia's Christmas Island National Park, creating a mesmerizing "ruby red rush hour" that has captivated tourists. According to Parks Australia officials, the massive crustaceans make their incredible trek from the dense forest to the coast to breed by the sea immediately following the first rainfall of the wet season. The event is such a massive draw for visitors—and so perilous for the millions of "creepy commuters"—that park officials proactively close roads and construct special crab bridges to help keep the animals safe during their journey.

articles.title_orig: The Metacritic Review Score Bar For ‘GTA 6’ Is Historically High
articles.title_zh: The Metacritic Review Score Bar For ‘GTA 6’ Is Historically High
articles.content_orig:
Reviews for Grand Theft Auto 6 are on the way from a batch of critics who reportedly had a whole lot of time to play it. While some are content to ignore Metacritic review scores, millions of gamers, loads of developers and overlord publishers very, very much care about them. And GTA 6 is going to be more scrutinized than almost any other game in history in that regard.
It’s hard to overstate just how high the bar is here for GTA 6’s Metacritic score . It essentially has to be one of the best-scored games of all time to match its predecessors, and even something like a low 90 would be considered a quality underperformance by some (I would argue unfairly, but this is the reality of the industry). So, what are the past scores here?
First of all, it’s hard to believe we got four huge Grand Theft Auto games in the span of seven years, from 2001 to 2008. Boy, have times changed. Second, you can see what I mean here: every GTA game from III to V , with Vice City and San Andreas in the middle, has a 95-98 score. I think we can agree that GTA 2 is not really a part of this conversation, and it came before the franchise really blew up.
More recently, GTA IV and V have gotten a 98 and 97, respectively. GTA IV is tied with SoulCalibur and Super Mario Galaxy 2 as the second-highest-scored game of all time (No. 1 is The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at a 99; the remaster currently has a 96). To put this in more context, out of 150 reviews on Xbox 360 and PS3, 75 of those are 10/10 scores.
If GTA 6 is below a 95 Metacritic score, I can guarantee you there is going to be an annoying narrative based on that. I do believe we have now entered an era of increased engagement bait and it is possible that some outlets or creators could sink it with a lower score just to stand out. Not that people have to like the game, but the last few years I have seen this happen repeatedly with other high-profile games, so keep that in mind. If someone gives GTA 6 a 5/10, that will probably be the most clicked-on review out of all of them.
Financially? No, it doesn’t matter. GTA 6 has 16 million pre-orders and over $1.5 billion in estimated revenue, and the game isn’t even out yet. It will be the fastest-selling game of all time and will try to someday surpass GTA 5 as the best-selling AAA game in history. A few Metacritic score points won’t matter. We cannot rule out the (very, very slim) possibility it may bomb, which would be a big deal, but needless to say, even if that doesn’t happen, expectations are sky-high based on the series’ history.
